title: The Complete Internet Journey Quiz
description: 20 questions tracing an end-to-end HTTPS request from URL entry, DNS resolution, ARP, routing, TCP handshake, TLS 1.3 encryption, to HTTP response rendering.

questions.question: When a user types `https://www.example.com` into a web browser address bar and hits Enter, what is the VERY FIRST operation executed by the browser before any network packet is dispatched?

options.text: Transmitting an ARP broadcast on the local Ethernet switch
Parsing the URL string, checking the browser's internal HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) preload list, and checking the local browser/OS DNS cache
Opening a TCP socket to root nameserver a.root-servers.net
Sending an HTTP GET request over raw IP

questions.explanation: Before generating packets, the browser validates the URL syntax, checks if HSTS forces HTTPS, and queries local memory caches (browser DNS cache, OS resolver cache, `/etc/hosts`).

questions.question: If the domain name is NOT found in the browser cache, OS cache, or hosts file, to what network entity does the operating system dispatch its DNS query?

options.text: To the Root Nameserver directly
To the Recursive DNS Resolver configured in network settings (typically assigned via DHCP)
To the website's web server
To the local switch's MAC table

questions.explanation: Stub resolvers on client endpoints forward recursive queries to a designated Recursive Resolver (e.g. ISP resolver, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) that performs the full iterative resolution walk.

questions.question: During the recursive resolver's lookup walk for `www.example.com`, which nameserver provides the referral delegation pointing to the `.com` TLD nameservers?

options.text: The Authoritative Nameserver for example.com
The DNS Root Nameserver (one of the 13 anycast root clusters)
The local home router
The Google Web Crawler

questions.explanation: The Root Nameservers hold the top of the tree. When asked for `www.example.com`, the root server replies with NS records pointing to the TLD servers responsible for the `.com` zone.

questions.question: Once the client obtains destination IP `93.184.216.34`, how does the OS determine whether to send the frame directly to the web server or to its Default Gateway?

options.text: It checks if the server port is 443 or 80
It performs a bitwise AND between destination IP and its own Subnet Mask; if the resulting network ID differs from its own local subnet, it routes via the Default Gateway
It sends a ping to the web server to test distance
It asks the DNS server for routing instructions

questions.explanation: `Local Subnet Check = (Dest IP & Subnet Mask) == (Host IP & Subnet Mask)`. If false, destination is remote, requiring forwarding to the Default Gateway.

questions.question: When constructing the Layer 2 Ethernet frame for an outbound packet to `93.184.216.34` via Default Gateway `192.168.1.1`, what is the destination MAC address placed in the frame header?

options.text: The MAC address of the remote web server (`93.184.216.34`)
The MAC address of the local Default Gateway router (`192.168.1.1`)
Broadcast MAC (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF)

questions.explanation: MAC addresses are strictly link-local and hop-by-hop. The packet retains Destination IP = `93.184.216.34`, but the Ethernet frame Destination MAC MUST be the local gateway router's MAC address.
questions.subtopic: L2 vs L3 Addressing in Transit

questions.question: If the host does not have the Default Gateway's MAC address in its local memory, what protocol is triggered immediately to discover it?

options.text: BGP
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol broadcast)
DHCP
TLS Handshake

questions.explanation: Before the Ethernet frame can be placed onto the wire, the host must resolve the gateway IP to a MAC address using an ARP Request broadcast.

questions.question: As the Ethernet frame passes through an intermediate Layer 2 Ethernet switch on the LAN, how does the switch determine which output port to forward it to?

options.text: It inspects the Destination MAC address and looks up the corresponding port in its MAC Address Table (CAM Table)
It recalculates the IP checksum
It decrypts the TLS application data
It queries the DNS server

questions.explanation: Layer 2 switches operate by inspecting the Destination MAC address and forwarding the frame out the specific port associated with that MAC in the CAM (Content Addressable Memory) table.

questions.question: When the packet reaches the Default Gateway router, what modifications are performed on the packet before it is forwarded out the WAN interface? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: The router decrements the IPv4 Time to Live (TTL) by 1
The router recalculates the IPv4 Header Checksum
The router performs NAT/PAT, rewriting the private source IP/port with its public IP/port
The router strips the incoming Layer 2 Ethernet frame and encapsulates the packet in a new Layer 2 frame for the WAN link

questions.explanation: Every routing hop decrements TTL, updates header checksum, strips old L2 framing and encapsulates into new L2 framing. A NAT gateway additionally rewrites source IP/port.

questions.question: In internet transit across ISP backbones, what mechanism do core routers use to perform Longest Prefix Match (LPM) lookups in nanoseconds at line rate?

options.text: Binary tree search in main DDR4 RAM
Hardware TCAM (Ternary Content Addressable Memory) in application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs)
Sequential linear search through an ASCII text file
Python dictionaries

questions.explanation: TCAM allows matching across 0, 1, and 'don't care' wildcard bits in parallel across all FIB entries in a single clock cycle, enabling wire-speed forwarding.

questions.question: Which protocol governs the inter-domain path selection between the user's ISP, transit carriers (Tier-1 providers), and the web server's hosting cloud network?

options.text: OSPF
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)
RIPv2
STP

questions.explanation: BGP is the de-facto exterior gateway routing protocol connecting autonomous systems (ASNs) across the global internet.

questions.question: Once packets reach the web server's network and firewall, what transport layer handshake is executed to establish a reliable connection before any HTTPS data is sent?

options.text: DHCP DORA 4-way exchange
TCP 3-Way Handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)
BGP Keepalive exchange
ARP Who-has query

questions.explanation: TCP establishes a full-duplex byte stream via SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK, establishing sequence numbers and flow control buffers.

questions.question: In TLS 1.3, how many round trips (RTT) are required for the cryptographic handshake to establish encryption keys before application data can be sent?

options.text: 3 RTTs
2 RTTs
1 RTT (Client sends ClientHello with Key Share; Server replies with ServerHello, Certificate, and Finished)
0 RTT is mandatory for all first-time connections

questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 reduced the handshake from 2 RTTs (in TLS 1.2) to just 1 RTT by combining the key share (Diffie-Hellman parameters) directly inside the initial `ClientHello` message.

questions.question: What is the role of the Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) and Certificate Authorities (CAs) during the TLS handshake?

options.text: They assign IP addresses to web servers

They allow the client to cryptographically verify that the server's public key belongs legitimately to `example.com` by validating digital signatures against pre-installed Root CA certificates in the OS/browser trust store
They compress the HTML before sending
They maintain the router's BGP routing table

questions.explanation: The server presents a certificate signed by an intermediate CA, leading up to a trusted Root CA embedded in the client's OS trust store. This prevents Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) impersonation attacks.

questions.question: Why does TLS use asymmetric public-key cryptography (like ECDHE) ONLY during the initial handshake, switching to symmetric cryptography (like AES-GCM or ChaCha20) for actual HTTP payload data?

options.text: Symmetric encryption is orders of magnitude faster and computationally cheaper on CPU hardware than asymmetric public-key operations
Asymmetric encryption cannot encrypt text, only numbers
Symmetric encryption keys are publicly visible on DNS servers
Asymmetric encryption does not work over Wi-Fi

questions.explanation: Asymmetric cryptography involves heavy modular arithmetic, which would overwhelm server CPUs at gigabit speeds. Hence, asymmetric keys are used only to securely negotiate a shared symmetric key, which AES hardware instructions encrypt in nanoseconds.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'Host' header sent in an HTTP/1.1 request (e.g. `Host: www.example.com`)?

options.text: It tells the router which gateway to use
It allows a single web server with one IP address to host hundreds of different websites (Virtual Hosting), routing requests to the correct virtual host
It specifies the user's MAC address
It disables TLS encryption

questions.explanation: Without the `Host` header, a web server hosting multiple domains on the same IP wouldn't know which website the client wanted. RFC 2616 made `Host` mandatory for virtual hosting.

questions.question: What HTTP response header instructs the browser to cache an image asset locally for 1 year without re-requesting it from the origin server?

options.text: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
Set-Cookie: session=active; ttl=31536000
Connection: keep-alive
Content-Encoding: gzip

questions.explanation: `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000` sets the browser cache expiry to 31,536,000 seconds (1 year). The `immutable` attribute signals that the resource will never change, eliminating conditional revalidation requests.

questions.question: When the browser receives the raw HTML response body, what critical parsing operations occur to turn text into pixels on the user's screen?

options.text: Generating the DOM (Document Object Model), CSSOM (CSS Object Model), combining them into a Render Tree, executing Layout (reflow), and Painting pixels to the screen
Writing the HTML directly into the router's ARP cache
Transmitting an ICMP Echo Reply to the DNS root
Converting the HTML into a BGP advertisement

questions.explanation: The browser parsing pipeline: Tokenize HTML -> DOM Tree; Parse CSS -> CSSOM Tree; Combine -> Render Tree -> Layout (compute geometry) -> Paint (rasterize pixels to GPU).

questions.question: What major performance advantage did HTTP/2 introduce over HTTP/1.1 to eliminate Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking at the application layer?

options.text: Binary framing and multiplexing of multiple concurrent request/response streams over a single shared TCP connection
Switching from IP to MAC routing
Eliminating all TLS encryption
Increasing maximum packet MTU to 9000 bytes

questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 required multiple parallel TCP connections or serial pipelining. HTTP/2 introduces binary streams, interleaving frames of multiple requests and responses concurrently over one TCP pipe.

questions.question: Why did HTTP/3 shift its underlying transport layer from TCP to QUIC (running over UDP)?

options.text: To make web pages load without internet access
To eliminate TCP-level Head-of-Line blocking (where one dropped packet stalls all multiplexed streams), and to combine the transport and cryptographic handshake into 0-RTT/1-RTT
Because UDP is more secure than TCP
Because TCP ports are deprecated by ICANN

questions.explanation: In HTTP/2 over TCP, if a single packet drops, TCP's in-order guarantee freezes all streams until retransmission completes. QUIC solves this by implementing independent stream loss recovery on top of UDP.

questions.question: When the browser finishes receiving all assets and the user closes the tab, how is the underlying TCP connection cleanly terminated?

options.text: The computer powers off
Via a 4-way handshake (FIN -> ACK, FIN -> ACK), and the socket enters TIME_WAIT to ensure all delayed duplicate packets drain
The switch clears its CAM table
An ARP broadcast is sent to clear DNS records

questions.explanation: The full lifecycle concludes with TCP's full-duplex teardown: both sides independently send FIN and acknowledge with ACK, with the active closer waiting out the TIME_WAIT interval.
